ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Progressive shortness of breath; no specific food, medication, or environmental trigger identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Dyspnea gradually worsening over ~2 weeks, noticeably worse in the last few days; now breathless walking to shops and around house.
- ENT symptoms: 
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation – denied  
  • Voice change/hoarseness – denied  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia – denied  
  • Drooling – denied  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms – denied  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing – denied  
  • Dyspnea – present, exertional; no positional component reported  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face) – denied  
  • Ear pain/hearing changes – denied  
  • Neck pain/swelling – denied
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: Known chronic heart failure; similar breathlessness and ankle swelling at initial HF diagnosis. No prior emergency visits or epinephrine use for airway issues.
- Allergies: “No allergies.”
- Current medications (dose/route/frequency not fully documented):  
  • Furosemide – patient unsure of dose (currently 1 tablet daily; plan to increase to BID)  
  • Aspirin – dose not documented  
  • Bisoprolol – dose not documented
- Social context: Lives alone with two cats; part-time lorry driver; ex-smoker; no alcohol use.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: Bilateral ankle edema (patient-reported); no facial, lip, tongue, or uvular swelling observed or reported.
- Airway/breathing: Patient able to converse in full sentences; no stridor or increased work of breathing noted.
- Mental status and associated features: Alert; no dizziness, syncope, or confusion reported.
- Vitals and examination findings: “Chest examination, oxygen saturations, and blood pressure all OK” (exact values not recorded).
- Presence of another person: None (patient alone during consult).

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression: Likely acute decompensated congestive heart failure presenting with exertional dyspnea and peripheral edema; no evidence of ENT-origin airway compromise.
  Evidence: Known HF, progressive SOB, new bilateral ankle swelling, mild dry cough; no ENT obstructive signs.
- DDx alignment (from reasoning system):
  1. Acute decompensated heart failure – high likelihood; matches history of HF with fluid-overload symptoms.
  2. Lower-respiratory tract infection precipitating/worsening HF – medium likelihood; dry cough and feeling “run-down,” but afebrile and chest exam normal.
  3. Pulmonary embolism – low-medium; sedentary occupation but timeline more gradual; no pleuritic pain or unilateral leg swelling.
  No current ENT-specific differential diagnoses suggested.

Plan:
- Immediate actions: Increase Furosemide from 1 tablet daily to 1 tablet twice daily for several days.
- Tests ordered: Blood work (CBC to screen for anemia/infection; renal profile) and outpatient echocardiogram.
- Patient instructions: 
  • Monitor for worsening breathlessness, new chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, or any throat tightness/voice change; seek urgent medical attention or call EMS if these occur.  
  • Continue current medications; take increased Furosemide as prescribed.  
  • Remain hydrated and record daily weights if possible (to track fluid status).
- Follow-up: Review in 1 week (earlier if symptoms worsen). Consider cardiology input based on echo results. No ENT follow-up required unless airway symptoms develop.
- Preventive/education: Encourage continued smoking cessation; discuss limiting salt intake to reduce fluid overload.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Exact vital signs, weight trend, orthopnea/PND history, full medication doses, documentation of baseline Furosemide dose and renal function, ENT airway examination details.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional minor dropouts but core clinical data intelligible.
